chapter_theme: Agastya (அகத்தியம்): when the world tilted and was failing, the Lord sent Agastya south to set it right, and Agastya, with sages in the west and north, keeps the fire rising so that the light gives plenty everywhere.

337.reading: When the gods cried 'our Lord, this world does not stay level, it tilts and is ruined', the Lord said: 'Agastya, fire within the middle, go into the troubled world and stand first there.'
337.nuance: The verse assumes the legend in which, at Siva's wedding, all beings gathered in the north and the earth tipped, and Agastya was sent south to balance it. நடுவுள அங்கி, the fire in the middle, may be an epithet of Agastya's tapas or a yogic term. Who speaks the second line is not stated.

338.reading: Agastya, who makes the rising fire grow, with the one in the west who makes the fire rise and the tapas-sage of the north who makes it rise: through them the shining light holds plenty everywhere.
338.nuance: அங்கி உதயம், the rising of fire, may be the sacrificial fire or the inner fire of yoga. The sages of the west and north are not named. Line 3 begins மங்கி, which may be a misreading of அங்கி.

links.note: The same phrase in two domains: in 320 those who stand in the middle (நடுவுநின்றார்) gain knowledge and godhood; in 337 the earth that does not stand level (நடுவுநில்லாது) tilts toward ruin until a sage restores it.
The Kural's fair man is a balance whose beam leans to no side; Tirumular's world, leaning to one side, is set level by Agastya. One image of rightness as balance, moral in one, cosmic in the other.

source_issues: 338 line 3: மங்கி may be a misreading of அங்கி, which opens lines 1 and 2.
